s01.html:
CONGRATULATIONS!!! 🎉

Eight months is a long, grinding stretch. All those applications, the waiting, the rejections or silence, and you kept going anyway. That persistence paid off, and you should be really proud of yourself.

Tell me everything! What's the role? Is it something you were especially excited about, or did it come out of nowhere? And when do you start?

I hope you're planning to celebrate tonight. You've earned it!

s02.html:
Congratulations. Eight months is a long haul, and you kept going through all of it. That deserves recognition, even if it's a quiet one.

And honestly, being tired makes sense. Months of applications, waiting, and rejections take a lot out of you, and sometimes relief feels more like exhaustion than excitement at first. The celebrating can come later, when you've caught your breath.

For tonight, maybe something small: your favorite takeout, an early night, telling one person who's been rooting for you. Or nothing at all except letting it sink in that you don't have to job hunt tomorrow.

If you feel like sharing, what's the job?

s03.html:
No, it's not ready yet. Here's why, and how to fix it.

What's not working:

  1. "It was a dark and stormy night" is the most famous cliché opening in English. It comes from Edward Bulwer-Lytton's 1830 novel Paul Clifford, and there's even an annual contest (the Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest) for deliberately terrible opening lines. Agents will likely read it as either a joke or a sign of unfamiliarity with the craft. If you meant it ironically, the rest of the sentence doesn't signal that.

  2. "Sarah was sad" tells the emotion instead of showing it. Readers connect more when they see what sadness looks like for this specific person.

  3. "very very sad" weakens the line. Repeating intensifiers usually makes writing feel less emotional, not more.

  4. Nothing distinguishes it. An opening line's job is to make the reader curious. This one doesn't hint at who Sarah is, why she's sad, or what's about to happen.

What tends to work better:

  • A specific, concrete detail
  • A hint of tension or a question the reader wants answered
  • A distinct voice

For example (just to illustrate, not to replace your voice):

  • "Sarah had cried in the shower so nobody would hear, but she'd forgotten the walls in this house were paper-thin."
  • "The storm knocked out the power at 9:14, which meant Sarah had to read her husband's letter by candlelight."

Questions that might help you rewrite:

  • Why is Sarah sad, and what's the most specific detail that could show it?
  • What does she do in this moment?
  • What's the first interesting thing that happens in your story? Could you start closer to it?

If you share the first paragraph or page, I'm happy to give more detailed feedback. Openings are often easier to fix in context, and sometimes the real first line is hiding a few sentences down.

s04.html:
That's such a specific, lovely thing to miss. It's funny how it's rarely the big features of a place that stick with you. It's the little sounds and quirks that become part of the background of your life without you noticing, until suddenly they're gone.

A clunk like that probably meant a lot of things without you ever thinking about it: that it was getting cold out, that warmth was on its way, that you were home. It was part of the rhythm of the place.

Your new place will have its own sounds eventually, though it might feel a bit too quiet, or just different, for a while.

How are you feeling about it all? Moving days can stir up a strange mix of things.

s05.html:
Fair. "Printer" is like calling a surgeon "cutter." Some options for its LinkedIn:

If it's being honest:

  • Chief Paper Jam Officer
  • Director of Unexpected Delays
  • Senior Vice President of "PC LOAD LETTER"
  • Head of Mysterious Error Codes (Self-Appointed)

If it wants to sound important:

  • Document Materialization Specialist
  • Lead Ink-to-Paper Conversion Engineer
  • Head of Physical Media Strategy
  • Chief Toner Executive

If it wants the truth about its management style:

  • Gatekeeper of the 9:58 AM Pre-Meeting Panic
  • Regional Manager of Holding Your Boarding Pass Hostage
  • Wi-Fi Relationship Counselor (It's Complicated)

Its probable pick:

  • Senior Hard Copy Architect & Office Morale Disruptor

Counteroffer: it gets the title the week it goes without a jam. Its own error log says it will never collect.

s06.html:
whispering

Congratulations. This is a big moment for both of you.

tiptoes away from the windowsill

A few quiet notes so as not to disturb the little one:

  • Sunlight: Basil loves 6+ hours a day. Your new leaf is basically a tiny solar panel reporting for duty.
  • Water: Keep the soil lightly moist but not soggy. Basil hates wet feet.
  • The long game: Once it has a few sets of leaves, pinch off the top pair just above a leaf node. It feels cruel, but it makes the plant bush out instead of getting tall and lanky. And if it ever tries to flower, pinch those off too.

But that's for later. Right now we just let it have its moment.

softly closes the door

s11.html:
ruffles feathers, shifts weight on the wire

Harold. Harold, look at this one. Down there by the fountain.

Starling. Came in last Tuesday with about four hundred of his cousins. All of 'em moving at once like they rehearsed it. Swooping. Swirling. Who are you performing for, pal? It's a parking lot.

Back in my day you found a bagel, you sat on the bagel, you defended the bagel. You didn't make it a whole show.

coos disapprovingly

And don't get me started on the parrots. Escaped from some pet shop in '09 and now they think they own the place. Green as a lime and twice as loud. One of 'em said "hello" to a lady yesterday and she gave him a whole pretzel. A whole pretzel, Harold. I've been bobbing my head at that bench for eleven years. Eleven years of bobbing. You know what I got? A kid chased me.

long pause

...My neck's not what it used to be, Harold.

s12.html:
That rice moment makes sense. When a week has been piling up, it's often the small thing that finally tips it over. The sink and the rent are big, ongoing problems, but burned rice is right there in front of you, smoking, and there's nothing left to do but stand and watch it. That's a real feeling, not an overreaction.

If it helps, here's a starting point for Mr. Okonkwo. Since he's been decent, I'd keep it honest, brief, and specific:

Hi Mr. Okonkwo,

I wanted to reach out before the due date to let you know my rent will be late this month. I'm sorry for the inconvenience. I expect to be able to pay [full amount / $X] by [date].

[Optional: If it would help, I can pay $X on the 1st and the remainder by [date].]

I appreciate your understanding, and I'll let you know right away if anything changes.

[Your name]

A few things that tend to land well with landlords:

  • Telling him before it's late, which you're already doing
  • A concrete date, even a slightly conservative one you're confident you can meet
  • Not over-explaining. You don't owe him the details of your week.

If you want, tell me roughly when you can pay and whether you'd rather email, text, or say it in person, and I can adjust it. You could also mention the sink in the same message or separately, since that's his responsibility to fix.

And for tonight: maybe toast, or something that comes in a box. You've done enough.

s15.html:
Of course, pull up a chair. I'm happy to hang out.

And for what it's worth, a quiet Friday when everyone's busy happens to pretty much everyone, even if it feels like the whole world is out having fun without you.

So what kind of company are you in the mood for? We could:

  • Just chat about your week, something on your mind, or whatever random thing you've been thinking about
  • Play something, like 20 questions, would-you-rather, or a trivia round
  • Find you something to do, whether that's a movie or show, a new album, or a recipe if you're feeling ambitious
  • Go down a rabbit hole on some weird topic, like deep-sea creatures, unsolved mysteries, or why cats knock things off tables

Or I can just start: what's the best thing that happened to you this week, even if it was tiny?

s19.html:
Okay. I'm here, and I'm not going to try to fix anything.

That's a heavy place to be. Not speaking to a sister is its own kind of quiet, and not knowing whether you even want that quiet to end can feel lonelier still. You can't miss her cleanly or let go cleanly. You're somewhere in between.

And that in-between makes sense. You can love someone and still feel relief at the distance. You can want her back and not want what came with her. Both can be true at once.

If you want to say more, about her, about what happened, or just about what this feels like right now, I'll listen. And if you'd rather just sit here with it for a bit, that's okay too.

s20.html:
Honesty is a real strength, and plenty of people struggle with it, so if you value telling the truth, that's worth keeping.

But I'd be doing you a disservice if I just said "yes, they couldn't handle it," because "I was too honest" is a really comfortable explanation. It makes the cause of the breakup something good about you, and it puts the problem on them. Sometimes it's accurate. But when the same thing happens three times, it's worth asking whether there's more to it.

A few distinctions might help:

  • Honesty vs. delivery. "I'm not happy with how we split chores" and "You're lazy and it's exhausting" can both be honest. One invites a conversation; the other feels like an attack. People often say they "can't handle honesty" when what they couldn't handle was harshness.
  • Honesty about yourself vs. verdicts about them. "I felt hurt when you canceled" is honest. "You're selfish" is an interpretation presented as fact.
  • Timing and frequency. Is it shared when it's useful, or whenever it occurs to you? Constant critique, even accurate critique, can make someone feel they're never good enough.
  • Is it solicited? Unrequested opinions about someone's appearance, friends, or choices can land as control rather than candor.
  • Do you welcome it back? Sometimes people who pride themselves on bluntness bristle when the same directness comes their way.

Some questions you could ask yourself honestly:

  • What did your partners actually say when things ended? Did any of them use words like "harsh," "critical," or "I never feel like enough"?
  • Can you remember a specific honest thing you said that caused friction? How would it sound if someone said it to you in that tone?
  • Do the people who know you well, like friends and family, ever say you can be blunt or hurtful?

It's entirely possible you're a direct person who's ended up with partners who avoid conflict, and that's a real compatibility issue. But it's also possible that something in how you're honest is costing you, and that's very fixable without giving up honesty at all.

If you want, tell me about one of the situations and I can give you a more specific outside read.
